Let $r = \lim_{N\rightarrow \infty}N_1/N$, $BB(\cdot)$ be a standard Brownian Bridge, and $\xi(\cdot)$ be a Gaussian Process with mean function $0$ and covariance function 
$
\text{cov}\{ \xi(x), \xi(y) \}  =  \sigma_0^2 f_0(x)f_0(y).
$ 
The limiting distribution of the SKS statistic is
$$
\sqrt{N}t_{SKS} = \sup_y\Big | \sqrt{N} \left\{     \widehat{F}_1( y+\widehat{\tau} ) - \widehat{F}_0(y)  \right\}  \Big|
 \stackrel{d}{\longrightarrow} \sup_y \Big |   \frac{1}{\sqrt{r}} SBB_1 + \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-r}} SBB_0  \Big|,
$$
 where $SBB_1(\cdot)$ and $SBB_0(\cdot)$ are independent realizations of the \textit{shifted Brownian Bridge} processes:
 $
 SBB(\cdot) \equiv BB(\cdot) + \xi(\cdot),
 $
 with covariance structure 
\[ 
\text{cov}\{ BB(x), \xi(y) \}= f_0(y) F_0(x)\{ 1\!-\! F_0(x) \}  \left[   E\{ Y(0) \mid Y(0)\leq x\} -  E\{ Y(0) \mid Y(0)  > x\}  \right] .
\]\label{thm::sks-nuisance} [Hypotheses: ass:constant-shift-null]

Because of this, much of the literature \citep[see, e.g.,][]{Cox:1984tx} defines a ``constant treatment effect'' as a statement that the marginal CDFs of the potential outcomes of the experimental  and control unit distributions $F_0(y)$ and $F_1(y)$  are a constant shift apart:
\begin{equation}
 H_0: {F}_1(y) = {F}_0(y - \tau) \qquad \mbox{ for some } \tau.  
\end{equation} Let $r = \lim_{N\rightarrow\infty}N_1/N$, and suppose $0<r<1$. Suppose the potential-outcome pairs are independent draws from a common joint distribution with continuous, nondegenerate marginals, and that, independently of those draws, a complete randomization assigns exactly $N_1$ units to treatment and $N_0$ to control. Suppose in addition that $F_0$ has a bounded uniformly continuous density $f_0$ and $E\{Y(0)^2\}<\infty$. Let $BB(\cdot)$ be a standard Brownian Bridge on $[0,1]$, and let $\xi(\cdot)$ be a Gaussian Process, jointly Gaussian with $BB\{F_0(\cdot)\}$, with mean function $0$ and covariance function $\text{cov}\{\xi(x),\xi(y)\}=\sigma_0^2f_0(x)f_0(y)$.

The limiting distribution of the SKS statistic is $$\sqrt{N}t_{SKS}=\sup_{y\in\mathbb{R}}\Big|\sqrt{N}\left\{\widehat{F}_1(y+\widehat{\tau})-\widehat{F}_0(y)\right\}\Big|\stackrel{d}{\longrightarrow}\sup_{y\in\mathbb{R}}\Big|\frac{1}{\sqrt r}SBB_1(y)+\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-r}}SBB_0(y)\Big|,$$ where $SBB_1(\cdot)$ and $SBB_0(\cdot)$ are independent realizations of the \textit{shifted Brownian Bridge} process $SBB(y)\equiv BB\{F_0(y)\}+\xi(y)$, with covariance structure \[\text{cov}\{BB\{F_0(x)\},\xi(y)\}=f_0(y)F_0(x)\{1-F_0(x)\}\left[E\{Y(0)\mid Y(0)\leq x\}-E\{Y(0)\mid Y(0)>x\}\right].\]

First, put $r_N=N_1/N$. We then have the exact identity \[\sqrt N(\widehat\tau-\tau)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{r_N N_1}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_1}\{Y_i(1)-\mu_1\}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{(1-r_N)N_0}}\sum_{i=N_1+1}^{N}\{Y_i(0)-\mu_0\}.\]

The independent sampling condition and $E\{Y(0)^2\}<\infty$ give $\widehat\tau-\tau=O_P(N^{-1/2})$. For the empirical-process remainder, the indicator class $\{I(Y(1)\leq y):y\in\mathbb R\}$ is Donsker. Its Gaussian limit is uniformly continuous in the semimetric induced by $F_1$; because $\widehat\tau-\tau=o_P(1)$ and $F_1$ is continuous, stochastic equicontinuity makes the displayed empirical-process increment $o_P(1)$ uniformly in $y$. The null gives $F_1(y+\tau)=F_0(y)$, and bounded uniform continuity of $f_0$ gives, uniformly in $y$, $F_1(y+\widehat\tau)-F_1(y+\tau)=f_0(y)(\widehat\tau-\tau)+o_P(N^{-1/2})$.

By definition of the empirical CDFs, the preceding expansion and the mean identity give, uniformly in $y$, \[\begin{aligned}\sqrt N\{\widehat F_1(y+\widehat\tau)-\widehat F_0(y)\}={}&\frac{1}{\sqrt{r_N N_1}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_1}\left[I\{Y_i(1)\leq y+\tau\}-F_1(y+\tau)+f_0(y)\{Y_i(1)-\mu_1\}\right]\\&-\frac{1}{\sqrt{(1-r_N)N_0}}\sum_{i=N_1+1}^{N}\left[I\{Y_i(0)\leq y\}-F_0(y)+f_0(y)\{Y_i(0)-\mu_0\}\right]+o_P(1).\end{aligned}\] Since $r_N\rightarrow r$, the two coefficients converge to $r^{-1/2}$ and $(1-r)^{-1/2}$.

More explicitly, set $\psi_y(a)=I(a\leq y)-F_0(y)+f_0(y)(a-\mu_0)$. The class $\{\psi_y:y\in\mathbb R\}$ is Donsker because it is the sum of the indicator class and the single square-integrable function $a-\mu_0$ multiplied by bounded $f_0(y)$. The treatment summands after shifting by $\tau$ and the control summands therefore each converge in $\ell^\infty(\mathbb R)$ to the centered Gaussian process $SBB(y)=BB\{F_0(y)\}+f_0(y)Z$, where $\operatorname{var}(Z)=\sigma_0^2$. Their covariance is $\operatorname{cov}\{BB\{F_0(x)\},f_0(y)Z\}=f_0(y)E[(I\{Y(0)\leq x\}-F_0(x))(Y(0)-\mu_0)]$, which equals the displayed conditional-mean expression. Conditional on an assignment of fixed group sizes, the two observed arm samples consist of disjoint independent potential-outcome pairs, and their joint law does not depend on which units were assigned. Hence the two process limits are independent, giving the joint limit used in the preceding display. The continuous mapping theorem applied to the supremum norm gives the limit of $\sqrt N t_{SKS}$ as $\sup_{y\in\mathbb R}|r^{-1/2}SBB_1(y)-(1-r)^{-1/2}SBB_0(y)|$. Each $SBB_j$ is a centered Gaussian process, so $-SBB_0$ has the same process law as $SBB_0$ and remains independent of $SBB_1$. Replacing $-SBB_0$ by this equal-in-law independent process gives the displayed plus sign.
